title: India's States Race to Lure Global Capability Centres Beyond Bengaluru as GCC Boom Reshapes Tier-2 Cities
excerpt: With 2,100 GCCs employing 2.36 million people and generating nearly $100 billion in revenue, Indian states are competing to attract the next wave of multinational tech hubs to cities like Noida, Nagpur, and Lucknow.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • India hosts over 2,100 Global Capability Centres, employing 2.36 million people and generating nearly $100 billion annually.
  • GCCs leased 16.5 million sq ft of office space in H1 2026, a 38% increase year-on-year.
  • States like Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra are promoting tier-2 cities with incentives to attract GCCs.
  • GCCs could add $155-199 billion in gross value over the next 3-4 years, impacting the economy by $450-600 billion.

  • India now hosts 2,100+ Global Capability Centres employing 2.36 million people and generating nearly $100 billion in annual revenue
  • GCCs leased 16.5 million sq ft of office space in H1 2026, a 38% year-on-year increase, accounting for 38% of total office leasing
  • States including Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Bihar, and Kerala are aggressively pitching tier-2 and tier-3 cities with policy incentives and talent pools
  • GCCs could contribute $155-199 billion in direct gross value added over the next 3-4 years, with total economic impact reaching $450-600 billion

Beyond Back-Office to Strategic Hub

India's Global Capability Centre industry is entering a new phase of expansion that could reshape the country's urban economic geography. At the CII GCC Summit in New Delhi, senior officials from Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Bihar, and Kerala outlined competing strategies to attract multinational investment beyond traditional hubs like Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Mumbai, and Pune.

The push reflects a fundamental evolution in what GCCs do. These centres have moved well beyond their original role as back-office support units and now handle strategic functions including artificial intelligence, data engineering, enterprise technology, and innovation, according to Rohan Lobo, Partner at Deloitte and Industry Leader for GCCs.

"If there is a significant amount of volatility, it is a driver of taking work from high expensive areas and bringing it into India where the cost savings are coming," Lobo said, noting that India offers a cost arbitrage of roughly two times compared to higher-cost markets. "In either of the cases, the industry will boom."

> **"Microsoft's India head Puneet Chandok pointed to the country's massive digital infrastructure, a talent pool of 27 million developers on GitHub, and policy openness that allows firms to scale quickly."**

"Microsoft's India head Puneet Chandok pointed to the country's massive digital infrastructure, a talent pool of 27 million developers on GitHub, and policy openness that allows firms to scale quickly."

The Scale Is Staggering

India is now the world's largest GCC hub, with more than 2,100 centres employing 2.36 million people and generating nearly $100 billion in revenue, according to a 2026 Nasscom-Zinnov report. The numbers continue to accelerate: GCCs leased approximately 16.5 million square feet of office space during the first half of 2026, a 38% year-on-year increase that accounted for 38% of total office leasing activity, according to Cushman & Wakefield.

Average office rents across India's top seven cities rose 9% year-on-year to Rs 96 per square foot per month in the first half of 2026, while vacancy levels fell to 15%, according to Anarock. The data confirms that GCC demand is outpacing new supply.

The Tier-2 Land Grab

As Bengaluru faces congestion, rising costs, and intense talent competition, states are positioning smaller cities as alternatives. Uttar Pradesh has emerged as a leading contender: Noida already hosts nearly 500 GCC units with 200-plus companies operating there, according to Alok Kumar, Principal Secretary for IT & Electronics.

Maharashtra is pushing beyond Mumbai and Pune to promote Nagpur, Nashik, and Chhatrapati Sambhaji Nagar. Bihar has introduced its GCC Policy 2026 with incentives linked to capital investment, rentals, and employment. Kerala is positioning itself through an AI-focused industrial strategy.

— Vimal Nadar, National Director & Head of Research, Colliers India

AI: Threat and Opportunity

Artificial intelligence is expected to automate 15-20% of current operational work carried out by GCCs. But Lobo argued that AI will simultaneously generate fresh opportunities by helping organisations identify technology issues, technical debt, and broken customer journeys, creating additional engineering work that could increasingly be executed from India.

The most critical talent shortages are in AI and data (41% of roles), platform engineering (39%), cloud and infrastructure (25%), and cybersecurity (18%), according to Quess Corp. These gaps are prolonging hiring cycles, especially for mid-senior roles outside tier-1 cities.

What This Means for NRIs

For Indians abroad, the GCC expansion signals continued career opportunities in India across high-value technology roles. Lobo estimated that GCCs could contribute between $155 billion and $199 billion in direct gross value added over the next three to four years. Including indirect contributions from supply chains and economic activity in sectors like real estate, healthcare, and education, the overall economic impact could reach $450-600 billion.

At several firms, Indian centres now lead global programmes and handle end-to-end work, from product development to complex commercial processes. Microsoft's India head Puneet Chandok pointed to the country's massive digital infrastructure, a talent pool of 27 million developers on GitHub, and policy openness that allows firms to scale quickly. For returning NRIs or those considering a move back, the GCC ecosystem increasingly offers roles that match Silicon Valley in scope, if not yet in compensation.
